title: The LEGO-style propaganda corpus
caption: Selected stills from fifteen distinct animations in the corpus, by provenance (rows) and upload date (left to right). Titles are shortened from the upload title or on-screen title; channel is the uploading account. Regime-linked videos are mostly re-uploads of animations credited to Explosive Media (Akhbar-e Enfejari) or other Iranian producers.
alt: Fifteen labeled stills from AI-generated LEGO-style propaganda videos, organized into regime-linked producers, Iran-aligned accounts, and trend adopters. These are study materials, not photographs of real events.
note: AI-generated LEGO-style propaganda reproduced and analyzed in the paper. These synthetic scenes are research material; they do not document real events. Provenance categories do not establish direct state control.

title: Selective suffering, fantasy, and circulation
caption: Tests of the H2 hypotheses. (a) Coefficient on an Iranian perpetrator in regressions of victim suffering among violent scenes with an identified perpetrator; the top rows use the standardized suffering index, the component rows its six elements on their own scales. (b) Within-video coefficients on scene type in regressions of fantasticality with video fixed effects. (c) Coefficients on standardized humor and alternative measures in circulation models; outcomes and estimators are identified by row. All intervals are 95 percent; standard errors clustered by video for fixed-effects models and by channel otherwise.
alt: Three original interval plots show lower depicted suffering for Iranian-perpetrated violence, small fantasticality differences by scene type, and no reliable within-channel humor–view association.
note: Outcomes measure representations in animated videos and collection-time engagement, not real-world suffering or causal persuasion.

title: Historical architecture, in game and in reference images
caption: Examples of image-based comparison of game architecture and real-world reference structures
alt: Labeled pairs compare in-game and reference depictions of the Dome of the Rock, Tikal, Salisbury Cathedral, Notre-Dame, the Statue of Zeus, Epidaurus, Stonehenge, Westminster Abbey, Palais Garnier, and Château de Chantilly.
note: Original game screenshots and reference images reproduced in the research paper. Architectural resemblance is only one dimension of historical representation.

title: Matching a building’s details across a photograph and a game
caption: LightGlue local feature matching approach.
alt: The paper’s LightGlue example links green architectural keypoints and orange correspondence lines between a real-world building photograph and its in-game representation.
note: Local feature correspondence illustrates a different measurement target from broad image resemblance; viewpoint and reference selection also affect the score.

title: From a courtroom frame to classifier probabilities
caption: The pipeline applied to one frame (2016 hearing). Note: In (d), the anger share is this face’s usual reading. Frame © ECHR-CEDH.
alt: An original four-panel figure shows an ECHR hearing frame, face detections, tracked identities, and expression-classifier probabilities over time. The probability labels describe model outputs, not judges’ feelings.
note: Facial-expression classifier outputs cannot establish a judge’s internal emotional state. Printed page19; PDF page20.

title: When head orientation changes an apparent party difference
caption: Head orientation and the difference between parties (exploratory). Note: (a, b) Same judges, one 2015 hearing. (c) Listening seconds. (d) Within judge-hearing, seconds with neither party speaking; bands = 95% CI. (e) Estimates with 95% CIs. Frames © ECHR-CEDH.
alt: Original ECHR frames compare judges facing each party. Histograms, response curves, and interval plots show that accounting for head orientation removes most of the apparent negative-display difference between government and applicant turns.
note: The orientation analyses are exploratory. These are classifier probabilities rather than direct measures of emotion. Printed page32; PDF page33.
